## What you will do

Notebook 1 gave you 400 **skeletons**: slots in the Ohio frame with a district,
a sex, an age, an ethnicity, a degree and a 2024 vote class, and nothing else.
A skeleton cannot be interviewed. This notebook gives each one a voice and then
asks it how it votes.

By the end you will have:

1. **matched** every skeleton to a real survey respondent: an Ohio respondent to
   the Cooperative Election Study (CES), 2020–2025;
2. **rendered** each twin as a persona, the text record the model reads;
3. **interviewed** the panel with the Talking to Machines vote module;
4. **aggregated** the answers and checked them against the certified 2024 result
   and the 2026 Senate polls.

### The objects, before any code

**Figure 2.1.** How one twin is built (A), and the three panels compared in Section 6 (B).

```{r objects-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "figures", "nb2_three_objects.png"))
```

**A twin is a skeleton plus a donor**, written out as one block of text called a
**persona**. The skeleton says *who* the person is: one cell of the census frame,
drawn in Notebook 1. The donor says *what they think*: one real CES respondent,
matched to the skeleton. Neither is a twin on its own.

**A civic record** is what a state voter file records about a registrant: their
county, the year they registered, which general elections they voted in, and
which primary ballot they last took. A registrant twin carries one. Yours
carries an empty one, because a synthetic skeleton has no voter-file row behind
it, and the persona says "not observed" rather than inventing it.

**Three panels, with fixed names.** Section 6 compares three things, and this notebook
keeps their names throughout:

1. **your panel**: 400 synthetic twins, built and interviewed here;
2. **the project's panel**: 4,000 real registrants from the Ohio voter file,
   with the same donors, persona template and vote module;
3. **the benchmark**: the certified 2024 result and the 2026 polling average.

Panels 1 and 2 differ **only** in where the skeleton comes from, so the gap
between them is what a voter file buys. Neither panel was fitted to the 2026
figure.

> **Where the attitudes come from.** The skeleton fixes *who* the twin is. Its
> values, issue positions, circumstances and media diet are **donated** by the
> matched respondent, and the persona says so line by line. The model is given
> this whole record and asked how *this* person would vote. It is not asked to
> make a person up.

**How to read this notebook.** As in Notebook 1, every table the code prints has
a number (Table 2.1, …), given in bold just above the code that prints it, and
the text says which table, row or column a number comes from.

The first block loads the R packages the notebook uses, sets the folders it
reads from (`data/`) and writes to (`output/`), and fixes the random seed.

```{r libs}
library(arrow)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(jsonlite)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
OUT  <- file.path("..", "output")
set.seed(20261013L)
```

## 1. Your panel

At this point, "your panel" is the 400 skeletons Notebook 1 deposited: no
donor, no persona and no answers yet. The block below loads them from
`output/oh_mini_panel_400.parquet` as a table called `panel`, and prints its
size and first three rows.

**Table 2.1.** `panel`, your 400 skeletons from Notebook 1: size, then the
first three.

```{r panel}
panel <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(OUT, "oh_mini_panel_400.parquet")))
panel[, vote2024 := as.character(vote2024)]
dim(panel)
head(panel, 3)
```

Table 2.1 is Notebook 1's Table 1.9 again, with two columns Notebook 1 added
later: `civic_record` ("not observed") and the rake `weight`.

Matching compares skeletons with donors, so the skeleton has to be described in
the donor pool's categories. These are coarser than the frame's: four age
bands, four ethnicity groups and a degree flag. They are used only to find a
donor.

The block below adds those four matching columns to `panel`: `sexk` (sex),
`age_band` (four bands, cut from `age`), `eth4` (Hispanic, Black, White, and
Other for everyone else) and `educ2` (degree or no degree). It then counts the
skeletons in each `eth4` group.

**Table 2.2.** `panel`: skeletons per matching ethnicity group (`eth4`).

```{r keys}
panel[, `:=`(
  sexk     = gender,
  age_band = as.character(cut(age, c(17, 29, 44, 64, 200),
                              labels = c("18-29", "30-44", "45-64", "65+"))),
  eth4     = fcase(ethnicity %in% c("Hispanic", "Black", "White"), ethnicity,
                   default = "Other"),
  educ2    = fifelse(college_grad == "Has a College Degree", "degree", "nodegree")
)]
panel[, .N, by = .(eth4)][order(-N)]
```

Table 2.2 shows how thin some groups are: 318 White skeletons, but only 21 in
`Other` (Asian, mixed-race, Native and other) and 14 Hispanic. That matters in
Section 3.

## 2. The donor pool

The donors are every Ohio respondent to the Cooperative Election Study (CES)
from 2020 to 2025: about ten thousand people, each with their own answers on
party, ideology, 53 harmonised issue items, circumstances, religion and media
use. The CES is a large academic survey of American adults, run every year.

The block below loads the pool as a table called `pool`, one row per
respondent. It gives each respondent a row number (`donor_row`), which the
matching uses to point at a donor, and counts respondents by survey wave and by
where their 2024 vote class comes from (`vote_class_from`).

**Table 2.3.** `pool`, the donors: respondents per CES wave, and the source of
their 2024 vote class.

```{r pool}
pool <- as.data.table(read_parquet(file.path(DATA, "oh_ces_donors.parquet")))
pool[, `:=`(donor_row = .I, sexk = sex)]
pool[, .(respondents = .N), by = .(wave = donor_year, vote_class_from = vote_source)][order(wave)]
```

The **2024 vote class** is a matching key, not an outcome. Each skeleton got its
class in Notebook 1, from the stage-2 model raked to the certified district
result, before any donor existed. A donor must share it, so donors need a class
too. Table 2.3 shows where each donor's class comes from:

- `ces2024_reported` (2,564 respondents): only the 2024 wave asked about the
  2024 vote, so these donors report it;
- `pid7_proxy`: for the other waves the class comes from **party
  identification** (the CES question `pid7`), with independents as "Other";
- `cl2020_validated_nonvoter_proxy` (870 respondents, 2020 wave): respondents
  with no validated November 2020 vote record stand in for 2024 stay-at-homes.

`pool` also carries a column called `donor_text`: the donor's half of the
persona, written out in advance for every respondent. It was produced with the
rendering code of the Talking to Machines Ohio panel, and that code was checked
against the panel's 4,000 personas: it reproduces their donor halves character
for character. The block below prints the first 900 characters of the first
donor's text.

**Text 2.1.** The start of one donor's `donor_text`.

```{r pool-text}
cat(substr(pool$donor_text[1], 1, 900), "...\n")
```

The header of Text 2.1 names the donor: the CES wave and the respondent's id.
Each line below it is one of the donor's own survey answers.

## 3. Hot-deck matching

Each skeleton is matched to a donor in its own cell, on five **nested keys**.
The algorithm tries the finest key first and falls back only when the cell
holds fewer than five donors:

| Level | Key |
|---|---|
| 1 | sex × age band × ethnicity × 2024 vote × degree |
| 2 | sex × age band × ethnicity × 2024 vote |
| 3 | age band × ethnicity × 2024 vote |
| 4 | sex × age band × ethnicity |
| 5 | age band × ethnicity |

Age band and ethnicity are in every key, so they always match. The vote class
drops out only at levels 4 and 5. Within a cell the donor is drawn at random.

The block below writes the five keys as functions (`K`) and the matching as a
function, `hotdeck()`. For each skeleton, `hotdeck()` looks for donors with the
same level-1 key; if there are at least five (`THIN_CELL`), it draws one at
random, and otherwise it tries level 2, and so on. It records the donor's row
(`donor_row`), the level it matched at (`level`), and how many candidate donors
that level offered (`n_candidates`). The result is a table called `matched`:
`panel` plus those three columns. The block prints how many twins matched at
each level, and the median number of candidates there.

**Table 2.4.** `matched`: twins per matching level, and the median number of
candidate donors (`median_cell`).

```{r match}
THIN_CELL <- 5L
K <- list(
  function(d) paste(d$sexk, d$age_band, d$eth4, d$vote2024, d$educ2, sep = "|"),
  function(d) paste(d$sexk, d$age_band, d$eth4, d$vote2024, sep = "|"),
  function(d) paste(d$age_band, d$eth4, d$vote2024, sep = "|"),
  function(d) paste(d$sexk, d$age_band, d$eth4, sep = "|"),
  function(d) paste(d$age_band, d$eth4, sep = "|"))
LEVEL <- c("1 sex.age.eth.vote.educ", "2 sex.age.eth.vote", "3 age.eth.vote",
           "4 sex.age.eth", "5 age.eth")

hotdeck <- function(skel, pool, seed = 20260913L) {
  set.seed(seed)
  idx <- lapply(K, function(f) split(pool$donor_row, f(pool)))
  key <- lapply(K, function(f) f(skel))
  pick <- function(cand) if (length(cand) == 1L) cand else sample(cand, 1L)
  res <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_len(nrow(skel)), function(i) {
    for (lv in 1:5) {
      cand <- idx[[lv]][[key[[lv]][i]]]
      if (length(cand) >= THIN_CELL)
        return(data.table(donor_row = pick(cand), level = lv, n_candidates = length(cand)))
    }
    cand <- pool[age_band == skel$age_band[i], donor_row]    # last resort: age band only
    data.table(donor_row = pick(cand), level = 6L, n_candidates = length(cand))
  }))
  cbind(skel, res)
}

matched <- hotdeck(panel, pool)
matched[, .(twins = .N, median_cell = median(n_candidates)), by = .(level = LEVEL[level])][order(level)]
```

Read Table 2.4 row by row: 385 twins match at level 1, 13 at level 2 and 2 at
level 3; none go further. A level-1 cell holds a median of 132 candidate donors
(the `median_cell` column), and one is drawn at random, which is what makes the
match a draw. The twins that fall back are in the thin groups of Table 2.2,
where the Ohio CES has few respondents; Table 2.6 below gives the share matched
at level 1 for each group. They lose the degree key first and then sex, but
never the vote class.

A donor can be drawn for more than one twin. The next block counts how often
that happens: how many distinct donors were used, the most twins any one donor
serves, and how many twins share their donor with another twin.

**Table 2.5.** Donor reuse.

```{r reuse}
matched[, .N, by = donor_row][, .(distinct_donors = .N, max_reuse = max(N),
                                  twins_sharing_a_donor = sum(N[N > 1]))]
```

**Exercise 3.1.** Which ethnicity groups fall back to a coarser key most often,
and why? Then compare each donor's vote class with its skeleton's. In this panel
no twin has a donor from a different class. Why must that be so? (Look at the
levels the twins matched at, and at the levels where the vote class leaves the
key.)

The block prints the share of each `eth4` group matched at level 1, then looks
up each donor's own vote class (`donor_vote`) and counts the twins whose donor
has a different class from the skeleton, with the deepest level any twin
reached.

**Tables 2.6 and 2.7.** Share matched at level 1 by group; donors from a
different class.

```{r ex-3-1}
matched[, .(twins = .N, share_level1 = mean(level == 1)), by = eth4][order(share_level1)]
matched[, donor_vote := pool$vote2024[donor_row]]
matched[, .(twins = .N, donor_class_differs = sum(donor_vote != vote2024), deepest_level = max(level))]
```

## 4. Render the persona

The twin's half of the persona is written here: the civic record and the
demographics. It follows the project's persona template line for line. Two rules
carry over from the project's panel:

- **Every line says where it came from.** A value labelled *census frame cell;
  modelled* was assigned from the skeleton's frame cell; nobody reported it. A
  value labelled *the matched survey respondent's own answer* is the donor's.
- **For three fields, ethnicity, education and income, the donor's own answer
  replaces the skeleton's modelled value.** In the project's panel the skeleton
  is a voter-file row, and a value the file actually records is kept. A synthetic
  skeleton has no file row, so all of its values are modelled, and on these
  three fields the donor's answer is the better information.

The civic record is where a synthetic twin differs most from a registrant twin.
A registrant carries an observed turnout history from the voter file (2016 to
2024 generals, primary ballots, registration year). A synthetic skeleton has
none, so the persona says so. It states 2024 turnout as **modelled**.

It never states the 2024 **vote choice**. Twin and donor share a 2024 vote class,
because the class is a matching key, but the persona does not say what it is.
The model has to work out the vote from the donor's party, ideology and issue
positions: that is Question A in Section 5.

The block below writes the persona as a function, `render_persona()`. It takes
one skeleton (`s`) and its donor (`d`) and writes the text line by line: the
civic record, the demographics (sex from the skeleton; ethnicity, education and
income from the donor), then the donor's `donor_text`. It runs the function for
all 400 twins, storing each text in a new column of `matched`, `persona_text`,
and checks that every persona contains its own donor's text. It prints how many
personas there are, their median length in characters, and how many are
identical.

**Table 2.8.** The 400 personas: count, median length, duplicates.

```{r render}
fld <- function(label, v) if (is.na(v)) sprintf("- %s: (absent)", label) else sprintf("- %s: %s", label, v)
SEX <- c(M = "Male", F = "Female")
LABEL <- "the state of Ohio"

render_persona <- function(s, d) {
  voted <- if (s$vote2024 == "stay") "no" else "yes"
  paste(c("=== PROFILE ===",
    sprintf("The following is a record describing an adult citizen in %s. It describes who you are: your", LABEL),
    "civic record, your circumstances, your values and your political opinions. Each section states where the", "information comes from.", "",
    "-- CIVIC RECORD (not observed: synthetic skeleton drawn from the census frame, no voter-file record) --",
    fld("Congressional district", s$cd),
    sprintf("- Voted in the November 2024 general election: %s (modelled from the census frame)", voted),
    "- Earlier general elections, primary participation, registration: (not observed)", "",
    "-- DEMOGRAPHICS (census frame cell; modelled fields marked, respondent's own answers marked) --",
    fld("Age", s$age), fld("Sex", paste0(SEX[[s$gender]], " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    if (!is.na(d$eth_ces)) fld("Ethnicity", d$eth_ces) else fld("Ethnicity", paste0(s$ethnicity, " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    if (!is.na(d$educ_ces)) fld("Education", d$educ_ces)
    else fld("Education", paste0(if (s$educ2 == "degree") "College degree" else "No college degree", " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    fld("Household income", d$income_ces),
    fld("Marital status", d$marital_ces), "",
    d$donor_text,
    "=== END OF PROFILE ==="), collapse = "\n")
}

matched[, persona_text := vapply(seq_len(.N), function(i) render_persona(matched[i], pool[matched$donor_row[i]]), character(1))]
stopifnot(all(mapply(grepl, pool$donor_text[matched$donor_row], matched$persona_text, fixed = TRUE)))   # each persona carries its own donor
matched[, .(personas = .N, median_chars = median(nchar(persona_text)),
            identical_texts = sum(duplicated(persona_text)))]
```

Table 2.8: 400 personas, a median of about 5,650 characters each, and none
identical. The next block prints one persona in full: the first level-1 twin
from the Democratic class.

**Text 2.2.** One persona, exactly as the model reads it.

```{r show-persona, comment = ""}
cat(matched[level == 1 & vote2024 == "D"][1, persona_text])
```

In Text 2.2, the `CIVIC RECORD` lines, `Age` and `Sex` come from the skeleton;
ethnicity, education, income, marital status and everything from
`VALUES & POLITICS` on come from the donor, each marked as the respondent's own
answer.

The donor's answers can disagree with the skeleton. The order is: the
skeleton's fields are fixed first, from the census cell; the donor then arrives
with its own answers on ethnicity, education and income; the donor's answer is
the one printed. Disagreement is expected rather than odd, because the match
used coarser versions of these fields: four ethnicity groups and a degree flag.
So a skeleton from a "no degree" cell can get a donor who reports a bachelor's
degree. The project counts these conflicts rather than hiding them.

The block below looks up each donor's degree flag (`donor_degree`) and counts,
at each matching level, the twins whose donor's degree differs from the
skeleton's.

**Table 2.9.** Degree conflicts between skeleton and donor, by matching level.

```{r conflicts}
matched[, donor_degree := pool$educ2[donor_row]]
matched[, .(twins = .N, degree_conflict = sum(donor_degree != educ2, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(level = LEVEL[level])][order(level)]
```

Table 2.9 shows no conflicts at level 1, where degree is part of the key, and
all of them at levels 2 and 3, where it is not. Ethnicity conflicts sit inside
the Asian, mixed-race and other groups, which share one matching category: an
Asian skeleton can get a donor who reports two or more races. Turnout is never
donated, so it never conflicts.

**Exercise 4.1.** Pick two twins with the **same skeleton cell** but different
donors, and read their VALUES & POLITICS sections side by side. How much of what
the model will read comes from the skeleton, and how much from the donor? The
block finds the first two twins that share a matching cell and prints both
personas up to the `CIRCUMSTANCES` section.

```{r ex-4-1, comment = ""}
twins <- matched[, if (.N >= 2) .SD[1:2], by = .(sexk, age_band, eth4, vote2024, educ2)][1:2]
for (i in 1:2) cat(sub("(?s)-- CIRCUMSTANCES.*", "", twins$persona_text[i], perl = TRUE), "\n\n")
```

## 5. The digital interview

This is the Talking to Machines **PoSSUM vote module**, here in R, with one call
per twin and two questions:

- **A.** Did this person vote in November 2024, and if so, with what
  probability for Harris, Trump or someone else?
- **B.** In the November 2026 special election for U.S. Senate in Ohio, with
  what probability do they vote for Sherrod Brown, Jon Husted, someone else, or
  not at all?

The model answers as a **third-person analyst** reading the record, in
**probabilities**, with no "not sure", and returns JSON checked against a fixed
schema. The prompts are the project's word for word except where the system
prompt describes the record. It says "one voter" rather than "one registered
voter", and no longer says the civic record comes "from the state voter file",
because here neither is true.

The block below sets up the interview and prints nothing. `MODEL` is the
language model; `API_URL` is where requests go; `SYSTEM` is the system prompt,
which tells the model its role; `QUESTION` is the two questions, added after
each persona; and `SCHEMA` fixes the shape of the answer: a yes/no for voting
in 2024, three probabilities for 2024 (`harris`, `trump`, `other`) and four for
2026 (`dem`, `rep`, `other`, `no_vote`).

```{r prompts}
MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
BASE <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL"); if (!nzchar(BASE)) BASE <- "https://api.openai.com/v1"   # on the workshop server, the course proxy
API_URL <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", BASE), "/chat/completions")
SYSTEM <- paste(
  "You are an experienced election analyst. You will be given the record of one voter: their civic record,",
  "demographics, and the values, party identification and issue positions of a survey respondent matched to them.",
  "Reason about how a person with this record would vote. Answer in the third person, as probabilities, never 'not sure'.",
  "Base the answer on the record only; do not assume anything about the campaigns beyond what is stated in the question.")
QUESTION <- paste0(
  "QUESTION A. In the November 2024 presidential election in Ohio, did this person cast a ballot (see the civic record), and if so, ",
  "what is the probability that they voted for Kamala Harris (Democrat), Donald Trump (Republican), or another candidate?\n",
  "QUESTION B. In the November 2026 special election for U.S. Senate in Ohio, the candidates are Sherrod Brown (Democrat) and ",
  "Jon Husted (Republican, incumbent). What is the probability that this person votes for the Democrat, ",
  "votes for the Republican, votes for someone else, or does not vote in that election? Weigh the person's own turnout history: ",
  "someone who has skipped recent general elections is unlikely to vote in a midterm.\n",
  "Return JSON only.")
probs <- function(...) list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = c(...),
                            properties = setNames(rep(list(list(type = "number")), length(c(...))), c(...)))
SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE,
               required = c("voted_2024", "vote_2024", "vote_2026"),
               properties = list(voted_2024 = list(type = "boolean"),
                                 vote_2024  = probs("harris", "trump", "other"),
                                 vote_2026  = probs("dem", "rep", "other", "no_vote")))
```

### Cached answers

Every twin in the seeded draw has already been interviewed once, and the answers
come with the notebook. This section therefore runs **offline, at no cost, with
the same result for everyone**. An answer is looked up by the twin *and* its
donor. If you change the seed in Notebook 1 or here, your new twins will not be
in the cache. With an API key they are interviewed live and saved to
`output/interviews_live.jsonl`.

The next block defines the helper functions and prints nothing:

- `ask_vote_module()` sends one persona with the questions to the model and
  returns its answer;
- `answer_key()` builds each twin's lookup key: twin id, donor's survey year and
  donor's respondent id;
- `norm()` and `flatten()` turn one answer into a row of numbers, rescaling
  probabilities to add up to 1 (a few answers come back in percent);
- `read_answers()` reads a file of answers into a table.

```{r interview-fn}
ask_vote_module <- function(persona_text) {
  body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low",
               messages = list(list(role = "system", content = SYSTEM),
                               list(role = "user", content = paste0("RECORD:\n", persona_text, "\n\n", QUESTION))),
               response_format = list(type = "json_schema",
                                      json_schema = list(name = "vote_module", strict = TRUE, schema = SCHEMA)))
  resp <- httr2::request(API_URL) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(body, auto_unbox = TRUE) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 4) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  c(fromJSON(resp$choices[[1]]$message$content),
    list(model = MODEL, in_tok = resp$usage$prompt_tokens, out_tok = resp$usage$completion_tokens))
}

answer_key <- function(d) paste(d$twin_id, pool$donor_year[d$donor_row], pool$donor_caseid[d$donor_row], sep = "|")
norm <- function(p) { p <- unlist(p); if (sum(p) > 0) p / sum(p) else p }   # a few answers come back in percent
flatten <- function(a) { v24 <- norm(a$vote_2024); v26 <- norm(a$vote_2026)
  data.table(voted_2024_llm = a$voted_2024,
             harris = v24[["harris"]], trump = v24[["trump"]], other_2024 = v24[["other"]],
             dem = v26[["dem"]], rep = v26[["rep"]], other_2026 = v26[["other"]], no_vote = v26[["no_vote"]]) }
NO_ANSWERS <- data.table(answer_id = character(), voted_2024_llm = logical(), harris = numeric(), trump = numeric(), other_2024 = numeric(),
                         dem = numeric(), rep = numeric(), other_2026 = numeric(), no_vote = numeric())
read_answers <- function(f) if (file.exists(f)) rbindlist(lapply(readLines(f), function(l) { a <- fromJSON(l); cbind(data.table(answer_id = a$answer_id), flatten(a)) })) else NO_ANSWERS
```

The next block runs the interview. It reads the cached answers
(`data/oh_syn_interviews.jsonl`) and any live ones, gives every twin in
`matched` its lookup key, and counts how many twins already have an answer. Any
twin without one is interviewed live, but only if an API key is set. Finally it
joins the answers to the twins in a table called `iv`, one row per interviewed
twin, and prints how many there are.

**Text 2.3.** The interview: answers found in the cache, and twins interviewed.

```{r interview}
CACHE <- file.path(DATA, "oh_syn_interviews.jsonl")
LIVE  <- file.path(OUT, "interviews_live.jsonl")
all_answers <- function() { a <- rbindlist(list(NO_ANSWERS, read_answers(CACHE), read_answers(LIVE)), use.names = TRUE); if (!nrow(a)) return(NO_ANSWERS); unique(a, by = "answer_id") }
matched[, answer_id := answer_key(.SD)]

answers <- all_answers()
todo <- matched[!answer_id %in% answers$answer_id]
cat(sprintf("%d of %d twins answered from the cache; %d to interview\n",
            nrow(matched) - nrow(todo), nrow(matched), nrow(todo)))

if (nrow(todo) > 0 && nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(todo))) {
    a <- ask_vote_module(todo$persona_text[i])
    cat(toJSON(c(list(answer_id = todo$answer_id[i]), a), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA), "\n", file = LIVE, append = TRUE, sep = "")
  }
  answers <- all_answers()
}
iv <- merge(matched, answers, by = "answer_id")
cat(sprintf("%d twins interviewed\n", nrow(iv)))
```

Text 2.3 should read "400 of 400 twins answered from the cache" and "400 twins
interviewed". Each row of `iv` is now a twin with its answers: `harris`, `trump`
and `other_2024` for 2024, and `dem`, `rep`, `other_2026` and `no_vote` for
2026.

---

## 6. What the panel says

Every answer is a probability, so a twin counts fractionally, and each twin
carries its rake **weight** from Notebook 1. The 2024 recall uses only twins
whose record shows a 2024 ballot, as the project does.

The first block loads the certified 2024 result by county and computes Harris's
statewide two-party share from it (`certified_harris_2p`, 44.3%). It prints
nothing; the number appears in Table 2.10.

```{r certified}
cert <- fread(file.path(DATA, "oh_county_certified_2024.csv"))
certified_harris_2p <- cert[, sum(sD * votes) / sum((sD + sR) * votes)]
```

The next block aggregates the answers. `voters` keeps the twins whose class is
D or R (the ones who voted in 2024). `recall` is their weighted Harris share of
the two-party vote, beside the certified share, with the difference in points.
`senate` is the whole panel's weighted 2026 turnout (one minus `no_vote`) and
Brown's share of the two-party vote.

**Tables 2.10 and 2.11.** Your panel's 2024 recall against the certified result;
its 2026 turnout and Brown share.

```{r aggregate, eval = nrow(iv) > 0}
voters <- iv[vote2024 != "stay"]
recall <- voters[, .(twins = .N,
                     harris_2p = sum(weight * harris) / sum(weight * (harris + trump)),
                     certified = certified_harris_2p)]
recall[, diff_pp := 100 * (harris_2p - certified)]
recall

senate <- iv[, .(turnout   = sum(weight * (1 - no_vote)) / sum(weight),
                 brown_2p  = sum(weight * dem) / sum(weight * (dem + rep)))]
senate
```

In Table 2.10, the 257 voting twins give Harris 46.0% of the two-party vote
(`harris_2p` 0.460), against a certified 44.3%: 1.7 points too Democratic
(`diff_pp`). In Table 2.11, the panel expects 66% turnout in 2026 and gives
Brown 47.2% of the two-party vote.

Does the model give back the class each twin was built with? The persona never
states the class, so the model has to infer it from the donor's values. The
block below calls each voting twin's answer Harris if its Harris probability is
at least its Trump probability (`llm_vote`), and prints, for the D and R
classes, the share the model calls Harris.

**Table 2.12.** The model's 2024 answer against the class each twin was built
with.

```{r agreement, eval = nrow(iv) > 0}
voters[, llm_vote := fifelse(harris >= trump, "D", "R")]
voters[, .(twins = .N, llm_says_harris = mean(llm_vote == "D")), by = .(frame_class = vote2024)]
```

In Table 2.12, the model calls 98% of D twins Harris voters and 3.5% of R twins.

Read this as a **manipulation check on the pipeline, not as evidence that twins
predict votes.** Every donor was matched on its twin's class, so the attitudes
the model reads were chosen to fit that class. High agreement shows the pipeline
kept what it was given. Notebook 3, Section 5 makes the same point about Model B, and
Notebook 3, Section 7 has the real test: an election that appears nowhere in the
pipeline.

### Your panel, the project's panel and the benchmark

The project's panel draws **4,000 real registrants** instead of synthetic
skeletons, and gives them an observed civic record. The block below puts the
three panels named at the top of this notebook side by side:

- **your panel**: the two numbers from Tables 2.10 and 2.11;
- **the project's panel**: its Ohio row in `benchmark_ohio.csv`, one of the
  panels Notebook 3, Section 7 shows;
- **the benchmark**: the certified 2024 result, and the RealClearPolitics
  polling average of 8–9 September 2026 (Brown 48.8, Husted 45.5).

**Table 2.13.** The three panels. All figures are the Democrat's share of the
two-party vote, in percent: Harris in 2024, Brown in 2026.

```{r vs-project}
# Benchmarks. 2024: certified result (MEDSL county returns, summed above).
# 2026: RealClearPolitics average of 8–9 September 2026, Brown 48.8 / Husted 45.5.
POLL_BROWN_2P <- 100 * 48.8 / (48.8 + 45.5)
bench <- fread(file.path(DATA, "benchmark_ohio.csv"))[panel == "oh_statewide"]

yours <- if (nrow(iv) > 0) c(100 * recall$harris_2p, 100 * senate$brown_2p) else c(NA, NA)
comparison <- data.table(
  panel         = c("Your 400 synthetic twins", "Talking to Machines: 4,000 registrants", "Benchmark: certified 2024 / RCP 2026 polls"),
  harris_2024   = round(c(yours[1], bench$harris_2p_twins, 100 * certified_harris_2p), 1),
  brown_2026    = round(c(yours[2], bench$dem_2p_2026_llm, POLL_BROWN_2P), 1))
comparison
```

Read Table 2.13 by column. In 2024 both panels sit about 2 points above the
certified result. In 2026 both sit well below the polls, which give Brown 51.7.
Notebook 3, Section 6 comes back to that gap.

## 7. Ask your own question

The scripted interview is fixed so everyone gets the same numbers. This cell is
yours. Put any question to any twin. It needs the API key set up for your
account and costs a fraction of a cent.

The block below defines `ask_free()`, which sends one persona and your question
to the model and prints the reply as plain text, then asks the first twin a
question. Change the persona (`matched$persona_text[1]`) or the question and run
it again. Without an API key the block is skipped.

```{r own-question, eval = nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))}
ask_free <- function(persona_text, question) {
  resp <- httr2::request(API_URL) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low",
      messages = list(list(role = "system", content = SYSTEM),
                      list(role = "user", content = paste0("RECORD:\n", persona_text, "\n\n", question)))), auto_unbox = TRUE) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  cat(resp$choices[[1]]$message$content, "\n")
}

ask_free(matched$persona_text[1],
         "Would this person support a state ban on cell phones in public-school classrooms? Answer in two sentences.")
```

## 8. Deposit

Notebook 3 post-stratifies these answers to the full Ohio frame (MrP). The block
below saves each interviewed twin, with its skeleton, weight, matching level,
donor ids and answers, to `output/oh_mini_panel_400_interviewed.parquet`, and
prints where it wrote the file.

```{r deposit, eval = nrow(iv) > 0}
keep <- c("twin_id", "cd", "gender", "ethnicity", "age", "age_bins", "college_grad", "vote2024", "weight",
          "level", "harris", "trump", "other_2024", "dem", "rep", "other_2026", "no_vote")
iv[, `:=`(donor_year = pool$donor_year[donor_row], donor_caseid = pool$donor_caseid[donor_row], stub = FALSE)]
out <- file.path(OUT, "oh_mini_panel_400_interviewed.parquet")
write_parquet(iv[, c(keep, "donor_year", "donor_caseid", "stub"), with = FALSE], out)
cat("written:", normalizePath(out, winslash = "/"), "\n")
```

---

## Where this comes from

The donor match, the persona template and the vote module are the ones
**Talking to Machines** uses for its digital-twin panels, including the PoSSUM
protocol (Protocol for Surveying Social Media Users with Multimodal LLMs). What
differs here is the skeleton: a census cell instead of a registrant, and a civic
record that says "not observed".
